en: Commentary on the Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree at Tianjie Shanushi Chan Temple during the Great Ming Dynasty.

The presiding monk Zongle, abbot of Yanfu Jangsi Temple, and the presiding monk Ruxi, having received the imperial decree, have together annotated this work based on the translation by Shi Hu. It records that the World-Honored One, while at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, entered the profound illumination and proclaimed the samādhi of the True Dharma.
Śāriputra addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"If there is anyone who wishes to practice and study this profound gateway of Prajñāpāramitā, how should they practice and study it?"
Thereupon, Avalokiteśvara proceeded to expound this sutra.
Since this sutra is the essential core of the great Prajñāpāramitā taught by the World-Honored One, it should be understood that what the Bodhisattva spoke is precisely what the Buddha spoke.
This teaching was transmitted to China through five translations in total; the version followed here is that translated by Xuanzang, as it is the one most widely prevalent in China.
"Prajñā" is a Sanskrit term; in the language of China, it means "wisdom."
Pāramitā, in the language of the Flower [China], means "reaching the other shore.
Sentient beings, due to being deluded regarding the nature of wisdom and dwelling in birth-and-death (saṃsāra), are called "this shore.
Bodhisattvas, by virtue of cultivating prajñā and awakening to the nature of wisdom, reach nirvāṇa; thus it is called "the other shore."
The "mind" refers to the *prajñā*-mind; this *prajñā*-mind is inherently possessed by every person.
Those who preach this sutra do so with the desire to cause sentient beings to sever deluded minds and manifest their original nature.
"Sūtra" means "Dharma" and "constancy.

This sūtra takes the singular Dharma as its name, the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its essence, contemplative insight as its central tenet, the deliverance from suffering as its function, and the Mahāyāna as its doctrinal characteristic.
These five points are all the essential teachings expounded in the sūtras.
"Single dharma" refers to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"True reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) refers to the empty nature of all phenomena.
"Contemplating and perceiving" means clearly seeing that the five aggregates are all empty.
"Delivering from suffering" means delivering [beings] from all hardships and calamities.
"The Great Vehicle" refers to the profound *prajñā* practiced by Bodhisattvas.
When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara practiced the profound *prajñāpāramitā*,
"Avalokiteśvara" refers to the bodhisattva who is able to cultivate *prajñā*.
"*Prajñāpāramitā*" refers to the dharma cultivated by the bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva, employing the wisdom of prajñā-observation, clearly perceives that his own mind is pure, perfectly integrated, and unimpeded; therefore, it is called "sovereign.
This is the practice for oneself.

Furthermore, he reflects upon sentient beings in the world who undergo suffering, causing them to cultivate this Dharma so that they may reform evil and transform toward goodness, leaving suffering behind to attain happiness, all with sovereign ease.
This is for the purpose of transforming others.
"Bodhisattva" is the Sanskrit term *bodhisattva*, which in the language of China means "one who awakens sentient beings.
To simply refer to them as "Bodhisattvas" is an abbreviation.
"Practice" (*yōgyō*) means cultivation.
"Deep Prajñā" refers to the Prajñā of the True Mark (*shissō hannya*).
It is not that which can be contemplated by those with novice minds or shallow wisdom; therefore, it is called "deep."
"Time" refers to the time when the Bodhisattva practices Prajñā.
"Illuminately seeing that the five aggregates are all empty, one transcends all suffering and calamity.
"Illumination" means contemplation.
The five aggregates (*skandha*) are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Aggregate" (*skandha*) means accumulation.
"Emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) refers to ultimate emptiness.
"Form" refers to the physical body.
"Feeling" refers to reception and experience.
"Perception" refers to conceptualization and thought.
"Formative activity" (saṃskāra) refers to the act of constructing;
"consciousness" (vijñāna) refers to discernment.
Consciousness is the sovereign mind (citta-rāja), while sensation (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and formative activities (saṃskāra) are mental factors (caitasika).
"Deliverance" means liberation.
"All sufferings and calamities" refers to the manifold sufferings of the world.
Because the Bodhisattva illuminates the emptiness and quiescence of the five aggregates, he is freed from the suffering of birth and death.

Furthermore, out of compassion for sentient beings who remain lost in delusion, whose inverted and false imaginings run counter to principle and disrupt the constant order, and who—through lack of loyalty and filial piety, and by committing the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes—undergo manifold sufferings, this Dharma-gate of Prajñā is taught so that they may practice it and all attain liberation.
The preceding section describes the meritorious deeds and practices of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva in saving sentient beings at the time when Ānanda compiled the Dharma-treasury;
this constitutes the separate introduction.
From the lower section beginning with Śāriputra, this marks the start of the response given by the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara to the questions of Śāriputra.
"Śāriputra! Śāriputra!
You are a disciple of the Buddha, foremost in wisdom."
Because he was asked by the assembly, the Bodhisattva called him by name and said:
"Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise thus.
Form is the illusory form of the four great elements, while emptiness is the true emptiness of *prajñā*.
Sentient beings, due to their delusion regarding true emptiness, undergo illusory form, just as water turns into ice.
By cultivating the wisdom of contemplation through *prajñā*, the Bodhisattva clearly perceives that illusory form is itself true emptiness, just as ice melts into water.

Since the substance of form and emptiness is no different, it is said that "form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form," just as ice is not different from water, and water is not different from ice.

Furthermore, fearing that sentient beings of dull faculties might not understand and would still maintain the dualistic views of form and emptiness, it is said: "Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form," just as ice is itself water, and water is itself ice.
Whether it be feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, none are otherwise.
This is the essential core of this sutra and the heart of Prajñāpāramitā. Śāriputra!
These dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness: they are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.
These "dharmas" refer to the aforementioned five aggregates (*skandhas*).
The characteristic of emptiness is precisely the true reality of ultimate emptiness.
The Bodhisattva further addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Since one has realized that all phenomena are, in their very essence, the true reality of ultimate emptiness, the essence of this true reality is fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing."
Since there is neither arising nor ceasing, how could there be defilement or purity?
Since there is neither defilement nor purity, how could there be increase or decrease?
Therefore, within emptiness, there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Within this true reality of ultimate emptiness, since it cannot be sought through arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, or increase and decrease, it is therefore summarized as being without form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; "without" (wu) signifies emptiness.
There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; there is no form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental object.
Within the true reality of ultimate emptiness, there are neither the five aggregates nor the six sense organs and six sense objects.
This emptiness refers to the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
There is no eye-element, and so forth, up to no mind-consciousness-element.
Since the twelve bases do not exist, neither do the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) exist.
The eighteen *dhātus* consist of the six sense organs (*indriya*), the six objects (*viṣaya*), and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).
The phrase "and so forth" indicates that while the beginning and end are mentioned, the middle is omitted.
As with the aforementioned five aggregates (*skandha*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and eighteen realms (*dhātu*), they do not transcend the two dharmas of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

For those whose delusion regarding the mind is predominant, it is taught as the five aggregates (pañcaskandha); for those whose delusion regarding form is predominant, it is taught as the twelve bases (dvādaśāyatana); and for those who are deluded regarding both form and mind, it is taught as the eighteen elements (aṣṭādaśadhātu).
Regarding the three sections above, a practitioner who trains according to their own faculties need only cultivate one section to achieve awakening and entry.
There is neither ignorance nor the exhaustion of ignorance, and so on, up to neither old age and death nor the exhaustion of old age and death.
This emptiness is the twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) refers to delusive darkness.

It means that one lacks clear understanding regarding the fundamental nature; it is not a state of total unconsciousness, but rather the term for a forced, distorted cognition that contradicts reality.

Regarding "no ignorance, etc.": the Bodhisattva, through the wisdom of *prajñā*, contemplates this ignorance and sees that its nature is fundamentally empty and devoid of the characteristics of arising and ceasing; therefore, it is said that there is neither ignorance nor the exhaustion of ignorance.

The statement that "there is no old age and death, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death" has the same meaning as before; it merely mentions the beginning and the end while omitting the middle.
As for the characteristic of birth, it is as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*: "Ignorance conditions volitional formations, and so on, until birth conditions old age and death."
Regarding the characteristic of cessation: as the Sūtra says, "With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; and so on, up to: with the cessation of birth, aging and death cease.
These twelve links of dependent origination are also called the twelve factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
The first is ignorance (*avidyā*), also termed affliction (*kleśa*).
The second is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), which refers to the performance of various karmas.
These two links are the causes produced in the past.
The third is consciousness (*vijñāna*), which refers to the arising of deluded thoughts at the initial moment of entering the mother’s womb.
The fourth is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which refers to the development of the sense organs and physical form after having entered the womb.
The fifth is the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), which refers to the formation of the six faculties within the womb.
The sixth is contact (*sparśa*), which refers to the engagement of the six faculties with the six objects after birth from the womb.
The seventh is feeling (*vedanā*), which means the experiencing of worldly matters such as the pleasant and the unpleasant.
These five links are the fruits experienced in the present life.
Eighth is craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which refers to the defiled attachment to the five objects of desire and so forth.
Ninth is grasping (*upādāna*), which refers to the arising of a mind of clinging toward various objects.
The tenth is "existence" (*bhava*), which refers to the cause of outflows (*āsrava*) that can summon future results.
These three links constitute the causes produced in the present.
Eleventh is birth (*jāti*), which refers to receiving a body composed of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in the future.
Twelfth is aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), which refers to the aging and dying of that future body once it has been received.
These two links are the fruits to be experienced in future lives.
These twelve links of dependent origination encompass the causes and effects of the three periods of time; they revolve one after another like a wheel, turning without ceasing.
It is truly lamentable that all sentient beings are deluded and do not realize this.

This is originally the realm contemplated by those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; Mahayana Bodhisattvas thoroughly illuminate this realm as being entirely devoid of substantial nature, and thus speak of it as "non-existent."
There is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path.
That there is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path means that one contemplates the purity of the Four Noble Truths.
Suffering refers to the fruit of suffering within birth and death; the origin refers to the causes of suffering, namely afflictions and karma. These two constitute the phenomena of the mundane world.

Cessation (*nirodha*) is the blissful fruit of *nirvāṇa*, and the Path (*mārga*) is the blissful cause consisting of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*); these two are supramundane dharmas.

The teaching of these Four Noble Truths is intended to cause sentient beings to know suffering, abandon its origin, aspire toward cessation, and cultivate the path, thereby leaving suffering behind and attaining bliss.

This is the realm contemplated by those who were originally śrāvakas; however, when a Mahāyāna bodhisattva illuminates and realizes this realm, they see that its very substance is empty and quiescent, and thus it is said to be "non-existent.
There is neither wisdom nor attainment.
"Wisdom" refers to the wisdom of *prajñā*.

When a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva illuminates objects with this wisdom, since the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and the various dharmas of the four truths (*catuḥsatya*) no longer exist, both person and phenomena are empty, and both object and wisdom are extinguished. It is like when the illness has departed, the medicine is forgotten; therefore, it is said that "there is neither wisdom nor attainment."
"Because there is nothing to be attained.
This phrase serves to conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one.

Because the Bodhisattva relies on the Prajñāpāramitā, his mind is without hindrance; because he is without hindrance, he has no fear; he is far removed from perverted dreams and delusions, and attains ultimate Nirvāṇa.
The Bodhisattva is the person who relies [upon the teaching];
Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma upon which one relies.
When a Bodhisattva practices and studies according to this gateway of Prajñā, their merit is perfected and the principle is revealed; thus, they attain a mind free from the bonds of karma.
Because there is no bondage of karma, there is no fear of birth and death.
Since there is no fear of birth and death, there are no inverted afflictions.
When these three obstacles are empty, the three virtues manifest; therefore, it is called ultimate nirvana.

Nirvana is the Sanskrit term *mahāparinirvāṇa*, which in the language of China means "Great Extinction and Deliverance" (*dà mièdù*). "Great" refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "Extinction" refers to liberation (*vimukti*); and "Deliverance" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*).

These three virtues do not exist separately; they are precisely the three obstacles. Delusion constitutes the three obstacles, while awakening constitutes the three virtues. That is to say: birth-and-death is itself the Dharma-body, afflictions are themselves Prajñā, and karmic fetters are themselves liberation.

Nevertheless, although the hindrances are themselves virtues, they cannot be manifested unless one possesses the merit of *prajñā*. This is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is exhausted, the clarity appears.
Such is what this means.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time—past, future, and present—rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā and thereby attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"The three periods of time" refers to the past, the future, and the present.
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, in the language of the flowers (Chinese), means "Unsurpassed Perfectly Equal and Right Enlightenment.

This statement implies that it is not only Bodhisattvas who cultivate and realize this in such a manner; rather, there are no Buddhas whatsoever who do not all cultivate Prajñā-pāramitā to achieve Perfect Enlightenment.
Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is the great divine mantra, the great illuminating mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, and the mantra equal to the unequaled.
The former is an explicit teaching of Prajñā, while the latter is a cryptic teaching of Prajñā.
Why, then, is it taught both explicitly and cryptically?
It is because the faculties and capacities of sentient beings differ, and thus the ways in which they enter [the path] vary accordingly.

Regarding the four kinds of spells, they refer to the functional efficacy of Prajñā: it is called the "Great Divine Spell" because it can destroy demonic obstacles; the "Great Illuminating Spell" because it can extinguish the darkness of ignorance; the "Unsurpassed Spell" because it can reveal the ultimate principle; and the "Spell Equal to the Unequaled" because its fruit of supreme wondrous awakening has no equal.
It is able to eliminate all suffering; it is true and not false.

The efficacy of this *prajñā* is vast and great; that it eliminates suffering and brings about happiness is certain and beyond doubt, causing all sentient beings to believe, accept, and practice accordingly.
Therefore, the mantra of the Prajñāpāramitā is spoken.
It is spoken as follows:
*gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*. Thus ends the secret exposition of the Prajñā.
This is one of the five reasons why [certain terms] are not translated.
For mantras are the secret language of the Buddha, unknown to ordinary beings.

The *Fahua shu* states: "Mantras are the names and titles of the kings of spirits; by invoking the name of their king, the tribes respect their lord, and thus one is able to subdue all malevolent ghosts and demons."
Some say that "mantra" (*dhāraṇī*) is like a secret code within an army: when the code is recited in accordance with its counterpart, there is no need for questioning or interrogation.
Furthermore, "mantra" means "aspiration," just as the *gongling* (a kind of wasp) invokes a blessing upon the *mingsing* (caterpillars), aspiring that they become like itself.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have spoken this mantra, wishing that all sentient beings may attain perfect enlightenment just as I have.
For those who are able to recite this mantra, there shall be no fulfillment of their aspirations that does not come to pass.
Annotated Commentary on the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra)
